## My Thinking

I've been farming this land for 30 years. I know this soil and I know what works. Quzhou gets dry summers and cold winters — my wheat-maize rotation is the backbone. The chili is my cash crop; the wheat and maize feed the family and cover basic costs.

My 10.1 mu breaks down like this in my head: 7 mu goes to the wheat-maize double-crop rotation — same land, back to back. The other 3.1 mu I put under chili. That chili money is what we depend on when the off-farm wages are slow.

**Wheat:** I'll plant in mid-October like always, after preparing the seedbed with rotary tillage. I use an improved Jimai-series variety — not the oldest seed my neighbors use, but not the expensive new stuff either. I split my nitrogen: base dressing at planting, topdress at jointing. Four irrigations — winter water in December to protect roots, then jointing, heading, and grain fill. Two pesticide passes for aphids and powdery mildew.

**Maize:** Right after wheat harvest in June, I direct-seed maize — no deep tillage, saves time and my back. I use a hybrid, Xianyu or Zhengdan, everyone around here does and yields are reliable. I topdress nitrogen at V6 and tasseling. Three irrigations depending on rain — jointing, silking, dough stage. The past few summers have been hotter, so I don't skip the silking irrigation.

**Chili:** This is where I spend the most labor. I transplant seedlings in late April. More potassium here — chili needs it for fruit quality. I irrigate more frequently because the roots are shallow and Quzhou summers burn. Four pesticide applications — bacterial wilt and spider mites are the main threats I've dealt with year after year. Some of my family helps during harvest, even the ones who work in town come back then.
